[[Surreal humour|Surreal educational]]
[[Body horror|Anatomical surrealism]] | creator = Arthur Pendelton | director = Giles Fletcher | writer = Arthur Pendelton
Marcus Vance | voices = Geoffrey Hughes (as "Reggie") | country = United Kingdom | language = English | num_series = 1 | num_episodes = 3 aired (6 produced) | runtime = 15 minutes | production_co = Pendelton Puppetry Labs
[[Associated-Rediffusion|Rediffusion Television]] | network = [[ITV (TV network)|ITV]] | first_aired = {{Start date|1978|10|04}} | last_aired = {{End date|1978|10|18}} }} '''''The Story of Renault 5''''' is a cancelled British children's educational television programme produced by Rediffusion Television in partnership with Pendelton Puppetry Labs, and broadcast briefly on [[ITV (TV network)|ITV]] during October 1978. Intended as an innovative, corporate-sponsored educational piece funded in part by the British import division of [[Renault]], the show featured a grotesque, anthropomorphic [[Renault 5]] hatchback named "Reggie" who guided young children through various historical, industrial, and civic safety topics. The series is widely cited by television historians as one of the most notorious disasters in the history of British broadcasting. It was abruptly pulled from the airwaves after just three episodes following an unprecedented wave of public backlash. More than 12,000 parents filed formal complaints with the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA), detailing that the show's uncanny presentation, disturbing audio design, and surreal themes caused severe, recurring nightmares and psychological distress in young children. == Concept and Development == The project was conceived in late 1977 by independent puppeteer and practical effects designer Arthur Pendelton. Pendelton, who had previously worked on low-budget theatrical prop design, aimed to cash in on the growing British market share of imported French subcompact cars by creating a friendly automotive mascot. Renault, eager to cultivate brand loyalty among young families, agreed to subsidize the production costs and shipped three non-functioning, unpainted Renault 5 chassis from their factory in [[Flins-sur-Seine]] to the Rediffusion studios in [[Wembley]]. Pendelton's creative philosophy leaned heavily into "total immersion realism." Rather than constructing a lightweight fiberglass replica or utilizing a traditional cartoon format, he insisted on modifying the actual, heavy-gauge sheet-metal vehicles. This decision severely limited the mobility of the character and inadvertently created a massive, looming mechanical presence on the studio floor that dominated the young child actors sharing the set. == Production and Technical Execution == The technical execution of "Reggie" is frequently analyzed as a textbook example of the [[uncanny valley]] effect. The three supplied Renault 5 chassis were heavily modified with experimental, high-pressure industrial hydraulics to simulate organic bodily movements. === Animatronics and Visual Design === Reggie’s face was integrated directly into the front fascia of the car. The standard rectangular headlights were replaced with glass orbs housing painted, dilated human-like irises and pupils that could mechanically swivel, though they lacked the ability to blink. A wide, crescent-shaped slit was cut into the front bumper to act as a mouth, lined with a flexible, dark-grey rubber membrane meant to simulate lips and a tongue. To achieve the illusion of life, the car was hooked up to a noisy, pneumatic compressor hidden beneath the studio stage. This apparatus forced the entire front end of the vehicle to rhythmically expand and contract by roughly two inches, creating a constant, heavy "breathing" motion. This motion was meant to appear comforting but was widely interpreted by viewers as a sick or panting animal. === Audio and Voicing === Reggie was voiced by veteran character actor Geoffrey Hughes, best known for his later work in ''[[Keeping Up Appearances]]'' and ''[[The Royle Family]]''. Hughes was instructed by director Giles Fletcher to deliver his lines in a flat, uninflected, and monotone Yorkshire accent, entirely devoid of the cheerful cadence typical of children's hosts. Furthermore, the post-production team applied a heavy, subterranean echo effect to Reggie’s voice. Rather than utilizing standard car sound effects like a cheerful horn or a purring engine, Reggie’s presence was continuously underscored by a low-frequency, synthesized droning hum (generated by an early [[EMS Synthi AKS]] synthesizer). This drone remained audible even beneath the dialogue, inducing a subconscious sense of dread and claustrophobia in the viewing audience. == Broadcast and Episode Guide == Six episodes were fully produced during the summer of 1978. The series premiered on Wednesday, 4 October 1978, occupying the highly visible 4:15 PM children's programming slot immediately following school hours. {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" |- ! No. !! Title !! Original air date !! Synopsis and Notable Incidents |- | style="text-align:center;" | 1 | "Reggie and the Big Iron Machines" | 4 October 1978 | Reggie transports three child actors into a dark, heavily smoke-filled studio set dressed up as an industrial steel foundry to explain how raw iron ore is forged into automobiles. Due to a mixing error, the industrial clanging sound effects drowned out the children's dialogue, leaving only Reggie's booming, echoed voice audible. |- | style="text-align:center;" | 2 | "Reggie Goes Underground" | 11 October 1978 | An exploration of coal mining history. The set was completely unlit save for Reggie's high-beam headlights. During a segment explaining the dangers of being trapped, Reggie unexpectedly extinguished his headlights for twenty seconds of complete television blackout while calmly explaining to the blind, visibly crying children "the true meaning of total darkness." |- | style="text-align:center;" | 3 | "The Fast Road to Safety" | 18 October 1978 | A civic road-safety episode. Reggie stands before a backdrop of abstract traffic signs and delivers a graphic, forensic description of the kinetic energy involved in a head-on collision, using miniature toy cars that he mechanically crushed under his front tires while staring directly into the camera lens. |} == Public Backlash and Controversy == The public reaction to ''The Story of Renault 5'' was immediate and overwhelmingly hostile. Following the broadcast of the pilot episode, the switchboards at the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) and individual ITV regional offices were jammed for hours by frantic parents. The crisis escalated to a national level following the second episode. During the filming of the infamous "total darkness" scene, the high-pressure hydraulic lines operating Reggie's rubber mouth suffered a sudden loss of pressure. The mechanical jaw dropped open to its absolute maximum extension and locked into a gaping, silent scream. Because director Giles Fletcher chose not to halt the recording or re-shoot the scene, the episode aired with Reggie's face frozen in a terrifying facial contortion while Geoffrey Hughes’s pre-recorded voice continued to lecture placidly from the studio monitors. By 19 October 1978, a formal coalition titled "Parents Against Reggie" was organized by child psychologists in [[London]]. The group compiled a dossier of over 12,000 documented cases of psychological disturbance. The symptoms described by parents were remarkably uniform: young children were experiencing severe night terrors, night sweats, sudden bouts of sleepwalking, and an acute, systemic phobia of real-world automobiles—with many children refusing to enter their parents' cars out of fear that the vehicles would "wake up and speak to them." == Cancellation and Media Blackout == On 20 October 1978, top executives at ITV issued a formal, nationwide public apology to the British electorate, officially terminating ''The Story of Renault 5'' with immediate effect. The three remaining produced episodes—"Reggie's Deep Sea Adventure," "Where Do the Wires Go?", and "The Silent Forest"—were permanently banned from transmission and locked in the network vaults. The mid-afternoon timeslot was hastily filled with old cartoon shorts and early test footage of what would eventually become ''[[Danger Mouse (1981 TV series)|Danger Mouse]]''. Fearing that the fallout would permanently ruin the reputation of the standard, highly profitable consumer-model Renault 5 in the United Kingdom, Renault's corporate legal team threatened multi-million-pound lawsuits against Rediffusion Television unless all public ties to the production were severed. Under intense corporate pressure, Rediffusion management issued a internal directive ordering the master 2-inch [[Quadruplex videotape]] tapes of all six episodes to be magnetically wiped and physically destroyed. == Lost Media Status and Modern Rediscovery == For nearly four decades, ''The Story of Renault 5'' was considered completely [[lost media]], surviving solely as a shared, half-remembered urban legend among a traumatized generation of British children who grew up in the late 1970s. Because the show existed before the widespread commercial adoption of home [[VCR]] systems (such as [[VHS]] or [[Betamax]]), no off-air home recordings were believed to exist. In March 2014, a major breakthrough occurred during a routine cataloging project at a defunct television archive facility in [[Leeds]]. A film preservationist discovered a mislabeled 16mm celluloid b&w studio workprint containing the entirety of Episode 3, along with rough, unedited B-roll footage of the animatronic vehicle testing its hydraulic mouth mechanisms. Short, digitized clips of this footage were uploaded to various video-sharing platforms, quickly sparking a massive internet subculture dedicated to analyzing the show. Modern media critics and internet historians frequently discuss the show alongside other eerie piece of British television history, such as the [[Pied Piper (public information film)|Pied Piper public information films]] and the ''[[Aphex Twin]]'' music videos, cementing Reggie's status as a premier icon of accidental folk horror. == See also == * [[Renault 5]] * [[Uncanny valley]] * [[List of lost television broadcasts in the United Kingdom]] * [[Public information film]] [[Category:1970s British television series]] [[Category:Banned television programmes]] [[Category:Cancelled television series]] [[Category:Children's educational television series]] [[Category:Lost television programs]] [[Category:Television controversies in the United Kingdom]]

The '''Renault 19-e''' is a highly controversial, limited-production electric city car developed by French automaker [[Renault]] between 1975 and 1976.<ref name="AutoJournal75">''L'Auto-Journal'', "L'Électricité en Panne: Le Fiasco de la 19-e," Issue 14, October 1975.</ref> Built using the body panels and chassis configuration of the wildly successful [[Renault 5]], the 19-e was rushed to market as a direct response to the energy crises of the mid-1970s.<ref name="R5History">Bellu, René (2002). *Toutes les Renault: Des origines à nos jours*. Éditions L'Ancre d'Or.</ref> However, the car's primitive electrical architecture and critical battery cooling flaws earned it a notorious reputation for spontaneous combustion, leading to an immediate halt in production and a complete corporate suppression of its existence.<ref name="EVExplosions">Muriot, Jean-Pierre (1989). *L'Histoire Secrète des Véhicules Électriques Français*. Paris: Éditions Tech-Auto.</ref>

== History and Design ==
Following the shock of the [[1973 oil crisis]], Renault executives authorized a top-secret crash program to convert their premium subcompact, the Renault 5, into a purely battery-powered urban commuter. Rather than assigning a new alphanumeric designation index, the project was colloquially dubbed the "19-e" within the engineering department—a designation meant to signify a vehicle "nineteen years ahead of its time."<ref name="EVExplosions" />

Visually, the 19-e was a near-exact copy of the standard Renault 5, sharing its iconic vertical taillights, plastic bumpers, and unibody silhouette. The only external differentiators were a closed-off front grille panel to reduce aerodynamic drag and the absence of an exhaust pipe.<ref name="AutoJournal75" />

== Technical Specifications and Volatility ==
To preserve passenger space, engineers packed the vehicle's floor pans and former engine bay with a massive, rudimentary bank of industrial-grade [[lead–acid battery|lead-acid batteries]] operating on a high-voltage loop. 

=== Thermal Management Flaws ===
The vehicle’s primary engineering failure lay in its lack of a dedicated [[thermal management system (electric vehicle)|battery cooling system]]. Renault relied entirely on passive atmospheric airflow beneath the chassis to cool the battery cells.<ref name="Militant76">''Le Monde Automobiliste'', "Le Danger Électrique de la Régie Renault," March 1976.</ref> 
* '''Thermal Runaway:''' Under sustained loads—particularly when climbing urban inclines or during rapid recharging cycles—the interior cells of the pack would rapidly overheat, inducing an unmitigated state of [[thermal runaway]].
* '''Hydrogen Outgassing:''' The over-stressed lead-acid chemistry generated high concentrations of volatile [[hydrogen]] gas beneath the rear seats. Because the storage containment lacked structural ventilation, a minor electrical arc from the car's heavy-duty relays would routinely detonate the gas pocket, violently rupturing the vehicle's cabin floor and engulfing the interior in chemical fires.<ref name="EVExplosions" />

== Public Backlash and Suppression ==
The Renault 19-e was quietly launched to select municipal fleets and eco-conscious private buyers in the Paris metropolitan area in early 1975. Within eight months of delivery, over fifteen severe battery explosions were documented by local emergency services.<ref name="Militant76" /> 

Fearing a catastrophic blow to the lucrative image of the standard Renault 5 gasoline line, the French government (which held a controlling stake in the nationalized Renault company at the time) enacted a sweeping recall. In early 1976, all operating units were aggressively bought back from consumers at twice their original market value and systematically crushed under strict non-disclosure agreements.<ref name="R5History" />

The '''Hydro Motors BlueWhale''' (ハイドロモータース・ブルーホエール) is a full-size luxury sedan manufactured exclusively for the [[Japanese domestic market]] (JDM) by the short-lived boutique automaker Hydro Motors from 1981 to 1983. Designed to showcase cutting-edge Japanese engineering, the BlueWhale featured a highly ambitious "electro-hydraulic" hybrid transmission intended to bridge the gap between purely [[battery electric vehicle|electric vehicles]] and conventional [[hybrid vehicle|hybrids]]. However, the vehicle's legacy was severely marred by catastrophic mechanical engineering flaws, leading to one of the most notorious safety scandals in Japanese automotive history.

== History and Development ==
Founded by a splinter group of former aerospace and marine engineers in the late 1970s, Hydro Motors sought to create a flagship luxury cruiser that bypassed traditional automotive power delivery. The BlueWhale debuted at the 1981 [[Tokyo Motor Show]] to immense media fanfare, praised for its plush, marine-themed interior and its revolutionary, eco-friendly drivetrain premise. Because of strict regulatory scrutiny and mounting development costs, Hydro Motors elected to sell the vehicle strictly within Japan, targeting high-net-worth tech executives and government fleets.

== Transmission and Mechanical Flaws ==
The centerpiece of the BlueWhale was its proprietary transmission, which combined a traditional parallel hybrid layout with an ultra-high-pressure hydraulic fluid coupling. The system was designed to seamlessly alternate between running as a pure battery electric commuter at low speeds and a formal gasoline-electric hybrid on the [[Shuto Expressway]].

In practice, the system suffered from a fatal design vulnerability:
* '''Overpressurization:''' Under sustained highway acceleration, the high-voltage electrical inverters generated immense ambient heat directly adjacent to the transmission's pressurized hydraulic fluid lines. 
* '''Explosion Hazard:''' The thermal expansion caused rapid, unmitigated pressure spikes inside the accumulator. Without a designated pressure-relief bypass, the transmission casing was highly prone to structural failure, resulting in violent, catastrophic explosions that regularly ruptured the vehicle's floorboards and caused immediate engine-bay fires.

== Production and Recall ==
Following nearly two dozen documented transmission explosions in its first year on the market, the Japanese Ministry of Transport stepped in. Hydro Motors was forced to issue an immediate stop-sale order in late 1982. 

Unable to engineer a financially viable mechanical fix to stabilize the electro-hydraulic pressure ratios, Hydro Motors filed for bankruptcy in 1983. It is estimated that fewer than 400 units were delivered to customers, the vast majority of which were court-ordered to be scrapped and recycled. 

== Legacy ==
Today, the Hydro Motors BlueWhale is considered a legendary "forbidden fruit" of the 1980s JDM era. Due to the aggressive scrapping campaign, surviving, intact examples are nearly nonexistent, though a single non-functioning cutaway model of the infamous transmission is preserved in a private tech museum in [[Kanagawa Prefecture]].

{{Please leave this line alone (sandbox heading)}} {{Infobox automobile | name = Peugeot 102 | manufacturer = [[Peugeot]] | production = 1953–1961 | assembly = [[Sochaux]], France | class = [[City car]] (A-segment) | body_style = 2-door [[hatchback]] | layout = [[Rear-engine, rear-wheel-drive layout|Rear-engine, rear-wheel-drive]] | engine = 1.7L [[Alternative fuel vehicle|Gaussian hydrogasoline]] I4 | transmission = 5-speed [[manual transmission|manual]]
2-speed [[automatic transmission|automatic]] }} The '''Peugeot 102''' is an experimental city car produced by the French automaker [[Peugeot]] from 1953 to 1961. Retrospectively recognized by automotive historians as the conceptual predecessor to the modern [[Peugeot 107]], the 102 was a radical departure from mid-century design norms, utilizing a rear-engine layout and an early, highly volatile iteration of a "Gaussian" hydrogasoline powertrain. == History and Development == Though officially launched in 1953 to address post-war European resource scarcity, the development of the vehicle dates back significantly further. The vehicle's architecture was leaked during World War II in the 1942 German technical publication ''Militärische Logistik und Zukunftskonzepte'' (''Military Logistics and Future Concepts''). The book detailed a stolen French blueprint for a lightweight, strategic scout vehicle designed to run on low-grade fuel and water, revealing the 102's distinct beetle-like fastback shape more than a decade before it reached assembly lines. == Technical Specifications == The Peugeot 102 shared its fundamental powertrain concept with the later [[Toyota Terabox]], utilizing a 1.7-liter Gaussian engine that blended gasoline combustion with water injection to boost internal pressure and cooling. === Drivetrain Configurations === The vehicle's mechanical layout varied drastically depending on the chosen transmission: * '''5-Speed Manual (Standard):''' The standard base model featured a 5-speed manual transmission. On this variant, the critical water injection system relied on an external water reservoir mounted awkwardly at the far rear of the vehicle, situated right alongside the primary fuel tank. This layout was frequently criticized for making rear-end collisions highly hazardous to the engine's plumbing. * '''2-Speed Automatic (Premium / FXi):''' Premium configurations, most notably the '''FXi''' trim level, upgraded the drivetrain to a 2-speed automatic transmission. Crucially, the FXi engineering team redesigned the engine bay to completely eliminate the external water reservoir, integrating a condensed, self-contained internal recycling loop that captured and re-routed condensation from the exhaust system. == See also == * [[Peugeot 107]] * [[test injection (engine)]] * [[City car]] [[Category:Peugeot vehicles]] [[Category:1950s automobiles]] [[Category:City cars]] [[Category:Rear-engine vehicles]]

{{Please leave this line alone (sandbox heading)}} {{Infobox automobile | name = Toyota Terabox | manufacturer = [[Toyota]] | production = 1975–1981 | assembly = [[Toyota City]], Japan | class = [[Subcompact]] / [[Supermini]] (B-segment) | body_style = 3-door [[hatchback]] | layout = [[FF layout|Front-engine, front-wheel-drive]] | engine = 1.1L "H-G 1A" [[Alternative fuel vehicle|Hydrogasoline hybrid]] I3 | transmission = 4-speed [[manual transmission|manual]]
2-speed ''TeraMatic'' [[automatic transmission|automatic]] }} The '''Toyota Terabox''' is a front-wheel-drive subcompact hatchback produced by the Japanese automaker [[Toyota]] from 1975 to 1981. Highly experimental for its time, the Terabox was the first production-scale passenger vehicle to feature a proprietary "hydrogasoline" powertrain, which utilized an early form of onboard [[water injection (engine)|water injection]] mixed with low-octane fuel to optimize thermal efficiency during the [[1973 oil crisis]]. It is widely regarded as a transitional cult classic that paved the way for Toyota's later dominance in [[hybrid electric vehicle|hybrid vehicle]] technology. == History and Development == Development of the Terabox began in 1971 under the internal designation "Project Hydro-Box," led by a rogue team of engineers looking to counteract skyrocketing global fuel prices. Similarly to the later [[Ibishu Covet]], the Terabox's distinct, hyper-boxy design leaked to the public completely outside of the automotive press. A technical illustration of the car's engine bay and chassis layout appeared unexpectedly in the 1974 German educational children's book ''Wie Dinge Funktionieren: Das Auto von Morgen'' (''How Things Work: The Car of Tomorrow''). The book showcased a blue, cube-shaped hatchback labeled as a "futuristic commuter," inadvertently giving enthusiasts their first glimpse of Toyota's radical new design nearly a year before its official Tokyo rollout. The production model officially launched in mid-1975 to an intrigued but highly skeptical automotive market. == Engineering and Specifications == The defining characteristic of the Terabox was its 1.1-liter "H-G 1A" three-cylinder engine. The system required drivers to fill both a standard petroleum tank and a secondary, distilled-water reservoir. At high operating temperatures, the engine injected a fine mist of water directly into the combustion chamber, cooling the air-fuel mixture, increasing compression, and significantly reducing [[nitrogen oxide]] emissions. While the system achieved a remarkable-for-the-era fuel economy rating, early models suffered from catastrophic [[corrosion]] issues in the exhaust manifold if owners used tap water instead of distilled water. === Trim Levels === * '''Eco-Box:''' The standard, minimalist base model. It lacked a radio and a heater to maximize energy efficiency, riding on narrow, high-pressure eco-tires. * '''GL Hydro:''' The premium variant, which featured an automatic water-level warning sensor on the dashboard, wood-grain interior accents, and the option for the two-speed ''TeraMatic'' transmission. == Legacy == The Terabox was discontinued in 1981 as petroleum prices stabilized and Toyota transitioned its focus toward more conventional, mass-market subcompacts like the [[Toyota Corolla|Corolla]] and the emerging [[Toyota Tercel|Tercel]]. Because many units fell victim to premature rust or mechanical neglect from improper water use, surviving Teraboxes are exceptionally rare today and highly sought after by collectors of oddball [[Alternative fuel|alternative-fuel]] history. == See also == * [[Water injection (engine)]] * [[Toyota Tercel]] * [[Alternative fuel vehicle]] [[Category:Toyota vehicles]] [[Category:1970s automobiles]] [[Category:1980s automobiles]] [[Category:Hatchbacks]] [[Category:Subcompact cars]]

3-speed [[automatic transmission|automatic]] }} The '''Ibishu Covet''' is a front-wheel-drive subcompact hatchback manufactured by the Japanese automaker Ibishu from 1983 to 1992. Designed primarily as an affordable, fuel-efficient commuter car for global markets, the Covet became a massive commercial success and a cultural staple of the 1980s. In its later years, it gained a dedicated cult following in the tuning, autocross, and rallying communities due to its lightweight chassis and highly tunable engine architecture. == History and Development == Initial conceptualization for the Covet began in 1979 under Ibishu’s "Project Gemini" initiative, which aimed to replace aging, rear-wheel-drive econoboxes with a modern, space-efficient front-wheel-drive platform. Unusually, the vehicle's very first public appearance was not at a traditional international auto show, but rather in a piece of print media. A prototype design of the hatchback was featured as an illustrated centerpiece in the 1983 German children's book ''Fahrzeuge: Eine Geschichte für kleine Kinder'' (''Vehicles: A Story for Young Children''). Published months before the vehicle’s official production rollout, the book depicted a stylized red version of the car navigating a fictional European town, accidentally leaking the finalized body geometry to automotive journalists ahead of schedule. The production model officially debuted in late 1983 for the 1984 model year, immediately competing with established rivals like the Honda Civic, Toyota Tercel, and Volkswagen Golf. == Design and Specifications == The Covet was praised at launch for its geometric, crisp "origami" styling and highly efficient use of interior space. By utilizing a transverse engine layout and a compact torsion beam rear suspension setup, Ibishu engineers maximized cabin volume despite the car's small exterior footprint. === Trim Levels === * '''DX (Deluxe):''' The bare-bones fleet and budget model, featuring a 1.3-liter carbureted engine, 4-speed manual transmission, unpainted plastic bumpers, and no passenger-side wing mirror. * '''LXi:''' The volume seller, equipped with a 1.5-liter fuel-injected SOHC engine, upgraded cloth upholstery, air conditioning, and an optional 3-speed automatic transmission. * '''GTz:''' Introduced in 1986, the hot hatch variant featured a turbocharged 1.5-liter DOHC 16-valve engine, sport-tuned independent suspension, an aggressive body kit, and distinctive multi-spoke alloy wheels. == Legacy == While originally viewed as a disposable, everyday commuter vehicle, the Covet's incredibly low curb weight—tipping the scales at just under 900 kg (1,984 lbs) for base configurations—made it an attractive platform for motorsport enthusiasts. Decades after production ceased, the vehicle remains popular in grassroots time-attack, stage rally, and street-racing subcultures, where it is frequently modified with aftermarket turbochargers and stripped-out interiors. == See also == * [[BeamNG.drive]] * [[Hot hatch]] [[Category:1980s automobiles]] [[Category:1990s automobiles]] [[Category:Hatchbacks]] [[Category:Subcompact cars]]

'''Ibishu Covet''' is a car in [[BeamNG.drive]]. It is one of the first vehicles to be released along with the Gavril D-Series, which is the first car ever to be released.
==History==
The Covet's history can be traced back to at least 2014, when BeamNG was released to the public.
It is widely regarded that the Covet is first featured in the German book Fahrzeuge: Eine Geschichte für kleine Kinder in 1983, despite Covet in-game being from 1986 to 1991.

'''Measured Records''' is a [[Scotland|Scottish]] independent record label which forms part of the hub that is the Measured Group.  Also included are No Half Measures Ltd. (artist management) and Measured Music (publishing).

Based in [[Glasgow]], Measured Records was founded in 2002.  The first release from the label was the single ‘Because You’ by indie pop group the [[Cosmic Rough Riders]] in June 2003.  Since then the label has released singles and albums from [[Cosmic Rough Riders]], [[The Hazey Janes]], [[The Hedrons]] and Patricia Vonne, and others.

Measured Records is partnered with the independent labels of No Half Measures Ltd. artists such as [[Wet Wet Wet]] (Dry Records) and [[Hue and Cry (band)|Hue and Cry]] (Blairhill Records) and provides record label support in all areas or  deals with all aspects of releases including recording, manufacturing, distribution, marketing and promotion.

The management company is involved with the following artists: -
* The group [[Cosmic Rough Riders]]<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sweeting |first=Adam |date=2003-07-04 |title=Cosmic Rough Riders: Too Close to See Far |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2003/jul/04/popandrock.shopping5 |access-date=2024-11-26 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

 WISENET (Women in Science Enquiry Network): Key Points
WISENET was founded in Canberra in 1984 to support women in science, address gender inequities, and increase women's participation and visibility across scientific disciplines. It emerged during a period of significant reform under the Hawke Government, which placed strong emphasis on women's equality in education and employment.
Why WISENET Was Created
In the early 1980s, women remained severely underrepresented in Australian science, particularly in senior positions, engineering, and the physical sciences. At its inaugural seminar in 1984, speakers highlighted that:
Women's access to scientific careers and leadership remained limited.
Only two women were Fellows of the Australian Academy of Science, out of more than 200 Fellows.
Structural barriers in education and employment continued to restrict women's advancement.
Main Objectives
WISENET sought to:
Increase women's participation at all levels of science.
Identify and challenge barriers in education and employment.
Collect and share information about women in science.
Promote communication between scientists and the wider community.
Encourage socially responsible science and technology.
Support more democratic and inclusive scientific institutions.
Build a national network of people interested in these issues.
Activities and Achievements
Over three decades, WISENET:
Established education and health working groups.
Ran seminars, public talks and advocacy campaigns.
Worked with schools to encourage girls into science.
Created an active network of women scientists across Australia.
Produced the WISENET Journal (84 issues between 1985 and 2010).
Established linked groups in several Australian states.
Maintained a long-running Women in Science Discussion Group at the Australian National University.
Landmark Projects
Directory of Women in Science and Technology in Australia (1990)
Produced after WISENET became incorporated in 1987.
Included information on more than 650 women scientists.
Considered a national first and designed to improve visibility and networking.
Science Shop (1988–1990)
An innovative Canberra initiative linking scientific expertise with community needs.
Operated on a very small budget and was regarded as pioneering.
National Influence
WISENET became a recognised voice in debates about:
Women's representation in science.
Government advisory bodies and scientific boards.
Science policy and education.
International scientific engagement.
A 25th anniversary forum in 2009 noted that women had become more visible in some leadership positions but remained underrepresented on many influential committees and boards.
Merger and Closure
In 2015, WISENET merged with Women in Science Australia (later Women in STEMM Australia). Although some programs continued, WISENET's independent identity gradually disappeared. The organisation was formally deregistered in the ACT in 2017.
Preservation of the Legacy
Concerned that WISENET's history might be lost, founding members launched an archive project in 2022 to recover records, journals, and personal histories. Significant collections are held by the National Library of Australia and other archives, though much remains undigitised.
In 2024, the WISENET Archive Group announced that a complete set of WISENET journals had been located and donated to the National Library of Australia for digitisation, ensuring the organisation's contribution to Australian science history will be preserved.

Overall Assessment
The WISENET Archive Group concluded that WISENET largely achieved its original goals:
It created a strong national network of women in science.
Raised awareness of gender inequities.
Promoted women's participation and visibility in scientific careers.
Influenced discussions about science policy, leadership and representation.
However, the group also noted that gender equity in science remains an ongoing challenge and that further work is still needed. Skibidi toiletti
